claim: Novice debugging help from general LLMs is partial and often wrong: GPT-3.5 names at least one real issue in 82-90% of help requests but all issues only 55-57%, and invents a non-existent issue in 40-48%.
agent_test: Run our agent on the same help-request set; score all-issues and false-positive rate at equal tokens with and without a verify-the-claimed-bug step.

claim: LLM error-message rewrites are fluent but frequently wrong: Codex gave comprehensible text 88% of the time but a correct explanation 48% and a correct fix 33%.
agent_test: Score explanation and fix correctness on the same 162-case grid; test whether an execute-and-check step raises fix correctness above 33%.

claim: Strong LLMs beat weaker ones on tutor-style debugging tasks but still trail human tutors, most on hints and grading feedback (GPT-4 hints 66% vs tutor 92%; grading match 16% vs 52%; repair 88% vs 100%).
agent_test: Reproduce the five-problem benchmark; compare plain model vs scaffold at equal tokens on hint quality.

claim: A separate validation stage raises precision of LLM feedback: GPT4Hints-GPT3.5Val reached about 95% precision at over 70% coverage versus about 60% for plain GPT-4 hints; fewer trials and a GPT-4 student validator lower both.
agent_test: Add a cheap independent validator pass to our agent; measure precision-coverage at equal tokens.

claim: Giving novices an AI code generator raises task success and speed during training (authoring correctness 80.1% vs 44.4%, d=1.67; time 210 s vs 361 s) but shows no reliable gain after the tool is removed (immediate post-test d=0.05; retention authoring d=0.28 p=.262; modifying d=0.41 p=.092). Gap-search update: a randomised N=78 study with a current model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) found that after AI access was removed, repair success was 23.1% with unrestricted AI versus 69.2% manual and 61.5% with a forced teach-back gate (p=.001); a CS1 crossover (Andleeb 2025) found speed and code-quality gains but mixed concept gains. All horizons are one session to a few weeks.
agent_test: Not directly an agent claim; as an analogue, test whether an agent scaffold that explains its fixes keeps its own gains when the scaffold is removed on held-out bugs.
audit_note: Kazemitabaar authoring 80.1 vs 44.4 (d=1.67), immediate post-test and retention figures consistent with the paper; Sankaranarayanan 23.1/69.2/61.5% p=.001 and Andleeb speed/quality gains with mixed concept gains verified at abstract level.

claim: Most novices use code generators as answer engines: 46% of tasks begin with a prompt, 92% of those with no own attempt, 66% paste the full task text; only 7% of uses were to fix code, and 61% of those localised the issue correctly.
schema_part: S0/S1 (force reading and localising before fixing)
agent_test: Compare agent that must state a hypothesis before editing against one that edits directly, at equal tokens.

claim: Weaker novices gain less or are harmed by AI help: struggling students overrated their own performance, metacognitive difficulty correlates with time (r=0.693) and course grade with time (r=-0.727); in Codex study gains in retention were concentrated in high prior-skill learners.
agent_test: Measure agent overconfidence on hard bugs: stated confidence vs correctness, with and without a calibration check.
audit_note: Evidence line for Kazemitabaar says low-skill learners gain more but the paper (RQ5, Sec 5.3) says high pre-test learners benefitted more on retention, matching the claim; Prather r=0.693 and r=-0.727 verified (n=21, small sample).

claim: Novices fix semantic bugs far more slowly than syntax bugs and brittle rule/knowledge breakdowns (fragile knowledge, the 'superbug' belief that the computer understands intent) underlie many failures.
agent_test: Seed bugs of semantic vs syntactic type and test whether a 'trace what the code does, not what it means' step helps.
audit_note: Henley confirms students took far longer on semantic than syntax errors (cited from an earlier study); McCauley handout only reached via a search summary (direct fetch 403), which matches superbug/fragile-knowledge claims.

claim: Teaching debugging explicitly helps novices: a classroom with a debugging-process unit fixed a median 4 of 9 bugs versus 2 for control (p=.049, n=13 vs 15) with higher self-efficacy; evidence is small-sample and non-randomised.
agent_test: Compare an explicit staged debugging process prompt to free-form at equal tokens.

claim: Socratic or teachable-agent designs improve novice outcomes in small trials: HypoCompass (n=19) improved scores p=.033 and cut time p=.003; TreeInstruct student fix rate +24.55%, and state grounding is critical (ablation -46.63% relevance). Gap-search update: a randomised N=132 trial found the Socratic AI TA with full context rated worst for task support and with the lowest full-comprehension share (48% vs 67% for Direct+Full; not significant); a fine-tuned planner cut premature answer disclosure from 7.43% to 1.88% of turns but plans were technically valid in only 11 of 53 cases.
agent_test: Test a question-first mode vs answer-first on LLM tutoring of seeded student bugs; small samples and simulated students limit transfer.

claim: LLM-generated reasoning that computes a concrete counterexample (reasoning trajectories) produces valid Socratic debugging dialogues: GPT-5 trajectory validity about 91% and Haiku-4.5 without reasoning 62.6%; reasoning mode helps smaller models more. Gap-search update (gap 7): in the Socratic debugging benchmark chain-of-thought raised GPT-4 manual F1 from 42.6 to 45.9 but cut GPT-3.5 from 22.2 to 8.5, so the benefit was larger for the bigger model, against the small-model claim; a counterexample-computing step was not tested there.
agent_test: Add a concrete-computation counterexample step to our agent and measure bug-localisation accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Frontier LLMs can diagnose and simulate novice misconceptions: diagnosis from a list 96.7-98.3% for top models vs 53.3% for Qwen2.5:7b; simulation follows misconception 90-96.7% for top models, 38.3% for the smallest; coder variants are not uniformly worse.
agent_test: Test an explicit 'what misconception would cause this bug' step on our agent; compare with plain debugging.

claim: LLMs can mine misconceptions in student code at scale (McMining: 82.0% multi-instance, 93.3% on bags with a misconception, 59.3% on correct-only bags), with weakness on correct code and subtle cases.
agent_test: Measure false-alarm rate of our agent on correct programs.

claim: Scaffold timing matters: in a 120-student study, teacher or learner-initiated reflection scaffolds scored 6.56-6.93 vs 4.06 for automatic scaffolds (F(3,116)=132.44), and cut the advantage of prior expertise. Gap-search update (gap 8): no replication of the initiation effect was found. A forced (automatic) Explanation Gate raised later repair success to 61.5% from 23.1% unrestricted, which does not match 'automatic scaffolds score worse', although the outcome measures differ.
agent_test: Compare agent reflection step triggered by an uncertainty signal vs always-on at equal tokens.

claim: Models degrade when code is in the question: text-davinci-003 scored 59.5% on code-containing MCQs vs 77.9% without (Savelka). StudentEval's 1,749 prompts from 80 novices show output depends heavily on prompt wording: a bare function signature with no docstring gives mean pass@1 of only about 0.05, so the student's description carries the task.
agent_test: Test a restate-the-spec step before debugging on code-heavy items.
audit_note: Savelka confirmed (text-davinci-003 59.5% with code vs 77.9% without, p<0.0001), but StudentEval's pass@1 0.0519 is a control for bare function signatures with no docstring, showing problems cannot be solved without the student's description, not a rate for wrongly specified student prompts.
claim_before_audit: Models degrade when code is in the question: GPT-3 family scored 59.5% on code-containing MCQs vs 77.9% without, and wrongly-specified student prompts yield very low pass rates (pass@1 about 0.05 for signatures without docstring).

claim: Murphy et al. 2008 and Fitzgerald et al. 2008 strategy counts remain unverified after the gap search: ACM and Taylor and Francis PDFs returned 403, no open copy was found, and the McCauley handout extract holds no counts. Only Crossref citation counts (42 and 147) were obtained.
agent_test: Obtain the papers via library and extract strategy counts.

claim: Fluent, readable LLM error explanations do not reliably speed up novice repair: GPT-4 explanations beat compiler messages in only 1 of 6 tasks (N=106), and in a crowd study (N=103) subjective ratings rose while fix rate, attempts and time did not improve significantly (novice fix rate 46% standard, 54% pragmatic, 42% contingent).
agent_test: Score our agent on whether its fix passes tests, never on explanation quality; compare readable-explanation prompts to terse ones at equal tokens.
audit_note: Santos and Becker (1 of 6 tasks, N=106) and Moraru et al. (N=103, novice fix rate 46/54/42%) verified; Moraru's rewrites came from llama-3.1-8B, not GPT-4, but the claim does not assert otherwise.

claim: Explicit prompt structure helps non-reasoning models localise novice bugs but not reasoning models: removing the novice description cost GPT-4 Top-1 by 38 to 78% on 50-program samples, while o3 and DeepSeekR1 were unaffected; error-type descriptions raised GPT-3.5 error classification from 35% to 56% (86 programs).
schema_part: S1-S5 (staged process may be redundant for strong reasoners)
agent_test: Run the staged scaffold and a free-form prompt on a reasoning and a non-reasoning model at equal tokens on seeded bugs; expect a gain only for the weaker one.

claim: Novice-program fault localisation accuracy by LLMs falls with problem difficulty and varies widely by model: o3 Top-1 was 62.0% on Condefects but 19.7% on Codeflaws (503 programs each); o3 per-bucket Top-1 ran from 71 (hardest) to 91 (easiest) on Condefects.
agent_test: Stratify the seeded misconception test set by difficulty and report per-stratum accuracy.

claim: Unrestricted AI help harms later unaided debugging, and an enforced explain-the-code step recovers most of the loss at a time cost: repair 23.1% unrestricted vs 61.5% gated vs 69.2% manual; gate median 14.2 minutes; novices who asked explanatory prompts fixed the bug (4.2 vs 0.4 prompts per session).
agent_test: Require our agent to state why a patch works before it is applied; measure regression on held-out bugs with the explainer removed.

claim: A planner that is not verified is a weak point in LLM tutoring: the fine-tuned planner produced a technically valid pedagogical plan in 11 of 53 cases, while GPT-4o with a separate verifier produced 53 of 53.
agent_test: Add a separate verifier to our plan step and compare invalid-plan rate with and without it.

claim: Current models answer general student questions at or above typical educator quality (mean 3.3 vs 2.9 of 5; 82% of Gemini 3 flash answers scored 3 or higher), but this was not tested for the false-issue rate on code help requests.
agent_test: Re-run the Hellas help-request set with a 2026 model and score false-issue rate.

claim: Qian and Lehman (2017) group novice difficulties into syntactic, conceptual and strategic knowledge, many rooted in prior knowledge (127 references); no per-misconception counts were obtained, so a seeded misconception set cannot yet be built from it.
agent_test: Stratify seeded bugs into syntax, concept and strategy classes.
